beats.act: cold open
beats.narration_text: Aloha — this is Liam, in for Divyank. A generated quiz question can look perfectly fine and still test the wrong thing entirely — passing every review while measuring nothing the chapter promised to teach. Let's build the assessments properly, then go hunt for exactly that failure.

beats.act: Act I — Three Reasons These Aren't Decoration
beats.narration_text: Quizzes aren't a formality bolted onto the end of a chapter. Being tested on material improves long-term memory more than re-reading it for the same amount of time — a real, replicated finding, not a study habit someone made up.

shot.prompt: real archival photo of students taking a computerized exam -- illustrative of the testing effect, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A1-1.source.txt

beats.act: Act I — Three Reasons These Aren't Decoration
beats.narration_text: Three assessment types, three separate findings behind them. Quizzes exploit the testing effect — retrieval practice. Flashcards exploit the spacing effect — study spread over time. Practice exercises push past recall toward actually applying what the chapter taught.

show.event: three chips snap in: Quizzes, Flashcards, Exercises

props.caption: each one earns its place from a specific finding

beats.act: Act I — Three Reasons These Aren't Decoration
beats.narration_text: The real citation: Roediger and Karpicke, 2006. Students who retrieved a passage from memory beat students who simply re-read it, on a test given one week later — roughly sixty-one percent versus forty percent.

show.event: citation card lands with the real figures

beats.act: Act I — Three Reasons These Aren't Decoration
beats.narration_text: The spacing effect is older, and just as real — memory improves when study is spread out over time instead of crammed into one sitting. The finding traces back to Ebbinghaus, in 1885, and has been replicated ever since.

shot.prompt: real archival vintage-pocket-watch photo -- illustrative of study distributed over time, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A1-4.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push onto the watch face
serif label lands: 'Ebbinghaus, 1885 — still replicated'

beats.act: Act I — Three Reasons These Aren't Decoration
beats.narration_text: Cram it into one sitting, or spread it out. Massed study feels more efficient and forgets faster. Spaced study feels harder and sticks — which is exactly what Anki's scheduling algorithm, S-M-2, from 1987, is built to enforce automatically.

show.event: question card: 'massed, or spaced?'
two outcomes: massed / spaced

beats.act: Act I — Three Reasons These Aren't Decoration
beats.narration_text: Generated matters too. The book eats its own dogfood — every question has to ground in the actual chapter text, or it isn't testing anything real at all.

beats.act: Act II — The Word For What's Wrong
beats.narration_text: To catch a bad question, you need a word for exactly what's wrong with it. That word is a level — and there are six of them, stacked, each one demanding more than the last.

beats.act: Act II — The Word For What's Wrong
beats.narration_text: Anderson and Krathwohl's 2001 revision of Bloom's taxonomy: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create. Six verbs, six rungs.

beats.act: Act II — The Word For What's Wrong
beats.narration_text: A learning outcome is written at a level — 'the reader can apply the build pipeline' is Apply. A question tests at a level too. The failure only shows up once you actually check them against each other.

beats.act: Act II — The Word For What's Wrong
beats.narration_text: The outcome says Apply. The question asks the reader to Remember a definition instead. It looks fine. It reads like a real quiz question. And it measures absolutely nothing the chapter promised to build.

beats.act: Act II — The Word For What's Wrong
beats.narration_text: That's the whole audit, in one move: never grade a question by itself. Grade it against the specific outcome it claims to serve.

beats.act: Act IV — What Goes Wrong
beats.narration_text: Four specific ways this exercise fails — and every one of them traces back to skipping the audit, not to a bad generator.

beats.act: Act IV — What Goes Wrong
beats.narration_text: Every question answerable from memory alone — the generator drifted to Remember. Flashcards that feel random — they were never grounded in the actual chapter text. You batched the whole book, then found systemic problems — you skipped the one-chapter calibration pass first.

beats.act: Act IV — What Goes Wrong
beats.narration_text: 'The audit found nothing' can mean two very different things. Either every question really is aligned — or you graded questions in isolation, never once checking them against the outcome they were supposed to serve.

beats.act: Act IV — What Goes Wrong

beats.act: verdict
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Three assessment types earn their place from real findings: quizzes from the testing effect, Roediger and Karpicke 2006; flashcards from the spacing effect, Ebbinghaus 1885, enforced by Anki's S-M-2 algorithm; and exercises from pushing past recall into application. Bloom's six levels — Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create — give you the word for what's wrong: a question that tests below the level its own outcome demands, passing every review while measuring nothing real. The real worked example: a generated question testing Remember when its outcome demanded Apply — fixed by rewriting it at the outcome's actual level, on the same topic. And every failure mode traces to skipping the audit — calibrate on one chapter first, and always grade a question against the specific outcome it claims to serve, never in isolation.

Run it. Liam, in for Divyank.
